subject: science

items.q: In the reactivity series, where is carbon placed?
items.correct: Between aluminium and zinc
items.misconception: Below gold, at the bottom
items.why: Learn carbon's rung: below aluminium, above zinc. Its place matters because carbon can take oxygen from the oxides of the metals below it.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

items.q: A piece of zinc and a piece of copper are put into separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. What would you see?
items.correct: Only the zinc gives bubbles
items.misconception: Only the copper gives bubbles
items.why: Use evidence from fair tests (same-sized pieces in the same acid or water), not the look of old objects. Aluminium is protected by its oxide coat; it is really more reactive than zinc, iron and copper.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

items.q: Which statement about the reactivity series is correct?
items.correct: Calcium is more reactive than iron
items.misconception: Iron is more reactive than sodium
items.why: Keep two ideas apart: hardness and strength describe how a material behaves when it is hit or pulled; reactivity describes how readily it reacts with water, acids and oxygen.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
items.random_wrong: Iron is more reactive than aluminium

items.q: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water. Which element reacts faster than magnesium with cold water?
items.correct: Calcium (Ca)
items.misconception: Carbon (C)
items.why: Check carbon's rung first. Carbon only wins the oxygen from a metal that is less reactive than carbon.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

items.q: Copper oxide powder is heated strongly with carbon powder. What does the carbon do?
items.correct: It takes the oxygen from the copper oxide
items.misconception: It burns to make heat that frees the copper
items.why: Follow the oxygen: it ends up joined to carbon in carbon dioxide. Without carbon, heating copper oxide or iron oxide does not give the metal.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.random_wrong: It joins on to the copper to make a compound

items.q: In a furnace, iron oxide is heated strongly with carbon. What are the products?
items.correct: Iron and carbon dioxide
items.misconception: Iron carbonate alone
items.why: Carbon takes the oxygen away from the metal. The metal is left on its own, and the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

items.q: Lead is less reactive than iron but more reactive than copper. Which statement about getting lead from lead oxide is correct?
items.correct: Carbon can extract it, as lead is below carbon
items.misconception: Carbon cannot extract it, as lead is unreactive
items.why: A reactive metal forms very stable compounds. The higher a metal is in the series, the harder it is to extract.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.random_wrong: Carbon can extract it, as carbon extracts any metal

items.q: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon, and the zinc oxide is reduced. In chemistry, what does 'reduced' mean?
items.correct: It has lost its oxygen
items.misconception: It has gained oxygen
items.why: Link 'reduced' to 'removed': a substance that is reduced has had oxygen removed.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

items.q: The diagram shows part of the reactivity series, with a new metal, X. How would metal X most likely be obtained?
items.correct: By electrolysis of a compound of X
items.misconception: By digging up pure X from rocks
items.why: Think of an ore as a rock containing a metal compound. Only metals at the bottom of the series, like gold, are found uncombined.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.random_wrong: By heating X oxide with carbon

items.q: In a furnace, zinc oxide and aluminium oxide are each heated strongly with carbon. Which metal is made?
items.correct: Zinc, but not aluminium
items.misconception: Aluminium, but not zinc
items.why: A reactive metal forms very stable compounds. The higher a metal is in the series, the harder it is to extract.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

items.q: Which statement about materials is correct?
items.correct: Ceramics are hard but can shatter
items.misconception: Metals are very good heat insulators
items.why: Metals let heat through quickly; a metal flask keeps heat in because of the vacuum between its two walls, not because metal insulates.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: A kettle case is too hard to be a polymer

items.q: Which of these statements is correct?
items.correct: Plastic bottles soften when heated
items.misconception: Tiles are so hard that they do not crack
items.why: Keep the words apart: hard (hard to scratch), stiff (hard to bend), tough (hard to break when hit), brittle (shatters). A material can be hard and brittle at the same time.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: Foam insulates, so it stays solid in a fire

items.q: A kiln heats pottery to over 1000 °C. Which material is best for lining the inside of the kiln?
items.correct: A ceramic, as it stays solid when very hot
items.misconception: A polymer, as it is a good heat insulator
items.why: Ask two separate questions: does it let heat through slowly (insulator)? does it stay solid when very hot (heat-resistant)? Most polymers soften when heated.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: A metal, as it is a good heat insulator

items.q: The diagram shows fibreglass: thin glass fibres held in a plastic. Compared with a sheet of glass, fibreglass is …
items.correct: much less likely to shatter when hit
items.misconception: weaker, because it is lighter than glass
items.why: Weight (or density) and strength are different properties. Composites are chosen because they are light and strong at the same time.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: just as soft and bendy as plastic

items.q: The diagram shows reinforced concrete: steel rods inside concrete. Concrete on its own cracks easily when it is bent. What do the steel rods do?
items.correct: They stop it snapping when it bends
items.misconception: Nothing, as it is just a mixture
items.why: Ask what the combination can do that neither part can do alone: fibres stop cracks spreading, so the composite is tougher than either part.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: They make it so hard it cannot crack

items.q: Does every metal react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.correct: No. Metals high in the series, such as magnesium and zinc, fizz in dilute hydrochloric acid; copper, silver and gold are too unreactive and give no bubbles.
items.misconception: Acids eat away any material, so every metal, even copper, reacts and fizzes in dilute acid.
items.why: Whether a metal reacts with a dilute acid depends on its place in the reactivity series. Copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does carbon mark the line between metals that react with dilute acid and metals that do not?
items.correct: No. Carbon's place is about extraction. Zinc and iron are below carbon but still react with dilute hydrochloric acid (zinc fizzes steadily, iron slowly). Only metals near the bottom, such as copper, silver and gold, give no bubbles.
items.misconception: Carbon marks the line between reactive and unreactive metals: every metal above carbon reacts with dilute acid, and no metal below carbon does.
items.why: Carbon's line is about extraction only. Reactivity falls gradually down the series, and zinc and iron still react with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Where does the oxygen from the metal oxide go?
items.correct: It joins with carbon to make carbon dioxide gas, which escapes. No oxygen is destroyed.
items.misconception: The oxygen taken from the metal oxide is destroyed or 'burnt away' by the heat, so it simply disappears and only the metal is left.
items.why: Atoms are never destroyed. The oxygen atoms are now joined to carbon atoms in carbon dioxide.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does 'reduced' mean that the substance has become smaller?
items.correct: No. In chemistry at KS3, a substance that is reduced has lost oxygen. A metal oxide is reduced when carbon takes its oxygen away.
items.misconception: 'Reduced' has its everyday meaning: the substance has become smaller or there is less of it.
items.why: Learn the science meaning: reduction is loss of oxygen; oxidation is gain of oxygen.
items.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Are all polymers soft and bendy?
items.correct: No. Many polymers are flexible, but some are hard and stiff, such as the plastic cases of kettles, hairdryers and plugs.
items.misconception: Polymers (plastics) are always soft and bendy, so a polymer cannot be hard or stiff, and a material containing a plastic is as soft as the plastic.
items.why: 'Polymer' is a family of materials with many different properties. Check the property needed; do not assume it from the name.
items.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented
